name: Dress watch

card.summary: A slim, minimalist formal wristwatch that finishes a suit or smart outfit.

quick.overview:
A dress watch is a thin, simple wristwatch meant for business and formal wear. It adds a refined accessory to an outfit and signals polish at the wrist.

Wristwatches became standard menswear in the early twentieth century, and dress watches descend from that tradition. Style references describe them as thin, plain and often gold or leather-strapped.
quick.how: People wear one with a suit, shirt cuffs or smart-casual outfit, usually on a leather strap, picking a slim case that slides under a cuff and a clean dial. Case size and strap colour are matched to shoes and belt.
quick.risks: There are few health risks; costs range widely, and a thin case offers less water and shock resistance than a sports watch.

lead: A dress watch is an elegant, minimalist wristwatch designed for formal and business attire, with a slim case, clean dial and few complications and a leather strap.[1]

Wikipedia describes traditional dress watches for business, semi-formal and formal occasions as gold, thin, simple and plain.[2] The wristwatch itself was originally mostly a women's item; men used pocket watches into the early twentieth century, and military use and the First World War popularised it.[2]
In looksmaxxing and style communities, it is treated as a finishing accessory.

chain: Slim formal watch under the cuff
angle.text: The watch is worn as part of a formal look. Its thin profile fits under a shirt cuff so the outfit stays clean.

paras: Dress watches prioritise understated refinement over sporty functionality, pairing slim cases with simple dials.[1] Some versions add a gemstone on the crown or faceted stones on the dial.[2]

Elizabeth I reportedly received an "armed watch" in 1571, and the oldest surviving wristwatch was made in 1806 for Joséphine de Beauharnais.[2] In 1904 Louis Cartier made a wristwatch for aviator Alberto Santos-Dumont, and Cartier still sells Santos-Dumont models.[2] Rolex's predecessor, founded by Hans Wilsdorf, was an early adopter of wristwatches in the 1910s.[2]
